danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Næste dag samledes tropperne på deres anviste pladser om aftenen og rykkede frem i løbet af natten. Det var en efterårsnat med mørke, purpurfarvede skyer, men uden regn. Jorden var fugtig, men ikke mudret, og tropperne marcherede lydløst; kun nu og da kunne artilleriets klirren svagt høres. Mændene havde forbud mod at tale højt, ryge pibe eller slå ild, og de forsøgte at forhindre deres heste i at vrinske. Foretagendets hemmelighed øgede dets tiltrækningskraft, og de marcherede muntert. Nogle kolonner, der troede, de havde nået deres mål, gjorde holdt, dannede våbenpyramider og slog sig ned på den kolde jord, men de fleste marcherede hele natten og ankom til steder, hvor de åbenbart ikke burde have været.

Kun grev Orlov-Denisov med sine kosakker (den mindst vigtige afdeling af alle) nåede sin anviste plads til rette tid. Denne afdeling gjorde holdt i udkanten af en skov, på stien der førte fra landsbyen Stromilova til Dmitrovsk.

Hen imod daggry blev grev Orlov-Denisov, der var døset hen, vækket af en desertør fra den franske hær, der blev bragt til ham. Det var en polsk sergent fra Poniatovskis korps, der på polsk forklarede, at han var løbet over, fordi han var blevet forbigået i tjenesten: han burde for længst have været udnævnt til officer, han var modigere end nogen af dem, og derfor havde han forladt dem og ønskede at hævne sig. Han sagde, at Murat tilbragte natten mindre end halvanden kilometer derfra, og at hvis de ville give ham en eskorte på hundrede mand, ville han tage ham til fange levende. Grev Orlov-Denisov rådførte sig med sine medofficerer.

Tilbuddet var for fristende til at blive afslået. Alle meldte sig frivilligt, og alle rådede til at gøre forsøget. Efter megen strid og diskussion besluttede generalmajor Grekov med to kosakregimenter at tage af sted med den polske sergent.
»Husk nu,« sagde grev Orlov-Denisov til sergenten ved afskeden, »hvis du har løjet, lader jeg dig hænge som en hund; men hvis det er sandt, skal du få hundrede guldstykker!«

Uden at svare steg sergenten med beslutsom mine til hest og red af sted med Grekov, hvis mænd hurtigt var samlet. De forsvandt ind i skoven, og grev Orlov-Denisov vendte, efter at have set Grekov af sted, tilbage, skælvende af den tidlige morgens friskhed og ophidset over det, han havde taget på sig på eget ansvar, og begyndte at betragte fjendens lejr, der nu netop var synlig i daggryets bedrageriske lys og de døende lejrbåls skær. Vore kolonner burde være begyndt at dukke op på en åben skråning til højre for ham. Han kiggede i den retning, men skønt kolonnerne ville have været synlige på lang afstand, var de ikke at se. Det forekom greven, at tingene begyndte at røre sig i den franske lejr, og hans skarpsynede adjudant bekræftede det.
»Åh, det er virkelig for sent,« sagde grev Orlov og betragtede lejren.

Som det ofte sker, når en, man har stolet på, ikke længere er inden for synsvidde, stod det ham pludselig helt klart og indlysende, at sergenten var en bedrager, at han havde løjet, og at hele det russiske angreb ville blive ødelagt ved fraværet af de to regimenter, som han ville lede Gud ved hvorhen. Hvordan skulle man kunne tage en øverstkommanderende til fange midt i en sådan troppemasse!
»Jeg er sikker på, at den slyngel løj,« sagde greven.
»De kan stadig tilbagekaldes,« sagde en fra hans følge, der ligesom grev Orlov følte mistillid til eventyrlysten, da han betragtede fjendens lejr.
»Nå? Virkelig... hvad mener du? Skal vi lade dem fortsætte eller ej?«
»Skal jeg lade dem hente tilbage?«
»Hent dem tilbage, hent dem tilbage!« sagde grev Orlov med pludselig beslutsomhed og kiggede på sit ur. »Det bliver for sent. Det er allerede helt lyst.«

Og adjudanten galopperede gennem skoven efter Grekov. Da Grekov vendte tilbage, besluttede grev Orlov-Denisov, ophidset både af det opgivne forsøg og af forgæves at have ventet på infanterikolonnerne, der stadig ikke viste sig, samt af fjendens nærhed, at rykke frem. Alle hans folk følte den samme ophidselse.
»Sid op!« kommanderede han hviskende. Mændene indtog deres pladser og korsede sig.... »Fremad, med Guds hjælp!«
»Hurra-a-a!« genlød det i skoven, og kosakafdelingerne slæbte deres lanser og rykkede frem den ene efter den anden, som hældt ud af en sæk, og stormede muntert over bækken mod lejren.

Et fortvivlet, forskrækket skrig fra den første franske soldat, der fik øje på kosakkerne, og alle i lejren, uklædte og netop vågnet, flygtede i alle retninger og efterlod kanoner, musketter og heste.

Havde kosakkerne forfulgt franskmændene uden at bekymre sig om, hvad der var bag og omkring dem, ville de have taget Murat og alt dér til fange. Det var, hvad officererne ønskede. Men det var umuligt at få kosakkerne til at flytte sig, når de først havde fået bytte og fanger. Ingen af dem lyttede til ordrer. Femten hundrede fanger og otteogtredive kanoner blev taget på stedet, foruden faner og (hvad der syntes vigtigst for kosakkerne) heste, sadler, dækkener og lignende. Alt dette skulle tages hånd om, fangerne og kanonerne sikres, byttet deles — ikke uden nogen råben og endda lidt indbyrdes slagsmål — og det var med dette, alle kosakkerne var beskæftiget.

Franskmændene begyndte, da de ikke blev forfulgt yderligere, at komme til sig selv: de formerede afdelinger og begyndte at skyde. Orlov-Denisov ventede stadig på, at de andre kolonner skulle ankomme, og rykkede ikke videre frem.

Imidlertid var, i overensstemmelse med dispositionerne, der sagde at »Første kolonne marcherer« og så videre, infanteriet af de forsinkede kolonner, kommanderet af Bennigsen og ledet af Toll, rykket ud i behørig orden og var, som det altid sker, nået et sted hen, men ikke til de anviste pladser. Som det altid sker, begyndte mændene, der var startet muntert, at gøre holdt; der hørtes murren, der var en følelse af forvirring, og til sidst en bevægelse tilbage. Adjudanter og generaler galopperede rundt, råbte, blev vrede, skændtes, sagde de var kommet helt forkert og var for sent på den, luftede lidt vrede, og til sidst opgav de det hele og marcherede bare fremad for at nå et sted hen. »Vi når nok et eller andet sted!« Og det gjorde de ganske rigtigt, skønt ikke til de rette steder; nogle nåede ganske vist til sidst deres rette plads, men for sent til at være til nogen nytte og kun i tide til at blive beskudt. Toll, der i dette slag spillede Weyrothers rolle ved Austerlitz, galopperede flittigt fra sted til sted og fandt alting på hovedet overalt. Således faldt han over Bagovuts korps i en skov, da det allerede var højlys dag, skønt korpset for længst burde have sluttet sig til Orlov-Denisov. Ophidset og ærgerlig over fiaskoen og i den overbevisning, at nogen måtte bære ansvaret, galopperede Toll hen til korpsets kommandør og begyndte at irettesætte ham strengt og sagde, at han burde skydes. General Bagovut, en drabelig gammel kampsoldat af roligt temperament, der ligeledes var oprørt over al forsinkelsen, forvirringen og modstridende hensigter, blev til alles overraskelse og stik mod sin sædvanlige karakter rasende og sagde ubehagelige ting til Toll.
»Jeg foretrækker ikke at modtage belæringer fra nogen, men jeg kan dø med mine folk lige så godt som enhver anden,« sagde han og rykkede frem med en enkelt division.

Da han kom ud på en mark under fjendens ild, gik denne tapre general lige fremad og førte sine folk under ild uden i sin ophidselse at overveje, om det at gå i kamp nu, med en enkelt division, overhovedet kunne tjene noget formål. Fare, kanonkugler og kugler var netop, hvad han havde brug for i sit vrede humør. En af de første kugler dræbte ham, og andre kugler dræbte mange af hans mænd. Og hans division forblev under ild i nogen tid helt unyttigt.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The next day, the troops assembled at their positions in the evening and advanced during the night. It was an autumn night with dark purple clouds but no rain. The ground was damp but not muddy, and the troops moved forward silently—only the occasional clinking of artillery could be faintly heard. The men were forbidden to talk aloud, smoke their pipes, or strike a light, and they tried to keep their horses from neighing. The secrecy heightened the adventure's appeal, and they marched cheerfully. Some columns, thinking they'd reached their destination, halted, stacked arms, and settled on the cold ground, but the majority marched all night and ended up in the wrong places.

Only Count Orlov-Denisov with his Cossacks—the least important detachment of all—reached his appointed position on time. His detachment halted at the edge of a forest on the path from the village of Stromilova to Dmitrovsk.

Toward dawn, Count Orlov-Denisov, who had dozed off, was woken by a French deserter being brought to him. It was a Polish sergeant from Poniatowski's corps who explained in Polish that he'd deserted because he'd been overlooked for promotion: he should have been made an officer long ago, he was braver than any of them, and so he'd left to pay them back. He said Murat was spending the night less than a mile away, and if they gave him a hundred men, he'd capture him alive. Count Orlov-Denisov consulted his fellow officers.

The offer was too tempting to refuse. Everyone volunteered, and everyone advised making the attempt. After much debate, Major-General Grekov set off with two Cossack regiments and the Polish sergeant.
'Now remember,' Count Orlov-Denisov said to the sergeant as he left, 'if you've been lying, I'll hang you like a dog. But if it's true, you'll get a hundred gold coins.'

The sergeant, without a word, mounted up with a resolute air and rode off with Grekov, whose men had quickly assembled. They vanished into the forest. Count Orlov-Denisov, having seen them off, returned, shivering in the freshness of early dawn and excited by what he'd taken on. He began scanning the enemy camp, now just visible in the deceptive predawn light and the dying campfires. The Russian columns should have been appearing on the open slope to his right. He looked that way, but though the columns would have been visible from quite far off, they were nowhere to be seen. It seemed to the count that something was stirring in the French camp, and his sharp-eyed adjutant confirmed this.
'Oh, it's really too late,' said Count Orlov, looking at the camp.

As often happens when someone you trusted is no longer in front of you, it suddenly seemed perfectly clear to him that the sergeant was a fraud, that he'd lied, and that the whole Russian attack would be ruined by the absence of those two regiments he'd sent off to God knows where. How could anyone capture a commander in chief from the middle of such a mass of troops!
'I'm sure that scoundrel was lying,' said the count.
'They can still be called back,' said one of his officers, who felt the same distrust as he looked at the enemy camp.
'Well? Really... what do you think? Should we let them go on or not?'
'Should I have them called back?'
'Call them back, call them back!' said Count Orlov with sudden decisiveness, looking at his watch. 'It'll be too late. It's getting light.'

The adjutant galloped through the forest after Grekov. When Grekov returned, Count Orlov-Denisov—stirred up by the abandoned attempt, frustrated by the infantry columns that still hadn't appeared, and energized by the enemy's nearness—decided to attack anyway. All his men felt the same excitement.
'Mount!' he commanded in a whisper. The men took their positions and crossed themselves. 'Forward, with God's help!'
'Hurrah!' echoed through the forest, and the Cossack companies, lances trailing, poured out one after another like grain from a sack and dashed merrily across the stream toward the camp.

One desperate, terrified shriek from the first French soldier who spotted the Cossacks, and everyone in the camp—undressed, barely awake—scattered in all directions, abandoning cannons, muskets, and horses.

If the Cossacks had pursued the French without worrying about what was behind and around them, they could have captured Murat and everything else. That was what the officers wanted. But it was impossible to budge the Cossacks once they had their hands on loot and prisoners. None of them listened to orders. Fifteen hundred prisoners and thirty-eight guns were taken on the spot, along with standards and—what mattered most to the Cossacks—horses, saddles, horse blankets, and the like. All this had to be dealt with: the prisoners secured, the guns claimed, the booty divided—not without some shouting and even a bit of fighting among themselves—and this was what kept the Cossacks busy.
The French, no longer being pursued, began to regroup and opened fire. Orlov-Denisov, still waiting for the other columns, advanced no further.

Meanwhile, according to the orders that said 'the First Column will march' and so on, the infantry of the late-arriving columns—commanded by Bennigsen and directed by Toll—had started out properly but, as always happens, ended up somewhere, just not where they were supposed to be. As always, the men set out cheerfully, then began to halt; grumbling was heard, confusion set in, and finally they started moving backward. Adjutants and generals galloped about, shouted, grew angry, quarreled, said they'd gone completely wrong and were late, vented their frustration, and finally gave up trying to follow the plan and just marched forward. 'We'll end up somewhere!' And they did end up somewhere, just not in the right places. A few eventually did reach their designated positions, but too late to be useful—just in time to be shot at. Toll, who played the same role in this battle as Weyrother had at Austerlitz, galloped tirelessly from place to place, finding everything in chaos everywhere. He stumbled upon Bagovut's corps in a wood when it was already broad daylight, though it should have joined Orlov-Denisov long before. Furious about the failure, assuming someone must be responsible, Toll galloped up to the corps commander and began berating him savagely, saying he ought to be shot. General Bagovut—a veteran soldier of calm temperament—was also upset by all the delays, confusion, and crossed purposes, and to everyone's surprise flew into a rage completely out of character, saying unpleasant things to Toll.
'I don't need lessons from anyone, but I can die with my men as well as anybody,' he said, and advanced with a single division.

Coming out into the open under enemy fire, this brave general marched straight ahead, leading his men into battle without considering, in his anger, whether attacking now with a single division would serve any purpose at all. The danger, the cannonballs, the bullets—that was exactly what he needed in his furious state. One of the first bullets killed him, and others killed many of his men. His division remained under fire for some time, entirely uselessly.
